title: Brain-Semantoks: Learning Semantic Tokens of Brain Dynamics with a Self-Distilled Foundation Model
claim: Instead of the usual pretrain-finetune-infer workflow, a self-distilled student-teacher pipeline turns noisy regional signals into network tokens and learns stable semantic representations through three losses.
layout: 2 parts: small vertical status-quo flowchart at left; large left-to-right pipeline with tokenizer inset, brain maps, time series on top, and student/teacher panels with loss arrows
description: The figure has three zones. At far left, a small 'Status quo' flowchart stacks Pretraining, Finetuning and Inference boxes with icons. A dashed arrow labeled 'Goal' skips from Pretraining straight to Inference. In the center, a boxed 'G: Semantic Tokenizer' inset shows a ROI-by-time series being mapped to networks and patchified. It then goes through a Multi-ROI Embedder. Brain-surface maps for regions and networks sit above and below it. At top right, multicolor fMRI time series are overlaid with red and blue boxes marking two long temporal views. These feed two large red-bordered panels, Student and Teacher, each stacking G, colored token squares, an f encoder, CLS tokens and h heads. Arrows between the panels are labeled L_Tok, L_TTR and L_CLS, with an EMA update and stop-gradient marks. The eye goes first to the colorful time series and the two big panels.
caption: Brain-Semantoks. A student-teacher architecture is used to learn stable brain dynamics representations across time by aligning long temporal views. The semantic tokenizer ($G$) is used to produce robust tokens of functional brain networks, which serve as input to a transformer encoder ($f$). Three losses are used during pretraining: a temporary regularisation loss for stability ($\mathcal{L}_{TTR}$), a within-view, latent space prediction loss of masked tokens ($\mathcal{L}_{Tok}$), and a global cross-view loss to learn a high-level, semantic representation ($\mathcal{L}_{CLS}$).
abstract: The development of foundation models for functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) time series holds significant promise for predicting phenotypes related to disease and cognition. Current models, however, are often trained using a mask-and-reconstruct objective on small brain regions. This focus on low-level information leads to representations that are sensitive to noise and temporal fluctuations, necessitating extensive fine-tuning for downstream tasks. We introduce Brain-Semantoks, a self-supervised framework designed specifically to learn abstract representations of brain dynamics. Its architecture is built on two core innovations: a semantic tokenizer that aggregates noisy regional signals into robust tokens representing functional networks, and a self-distillation objective that enforces representational stability across time. We show that this objective is stabilized through a novel training curriculum, ensuring the model robustly learns meaningful features from low signal-to-noise time series. We demonstrate that learned representations enable strong performance on a variety of downstream tasks even when only using a linear probe. Furthermore, we provide comprehensive scaling analyses indicating more unlabeled data reliably results in out-of-distribution performance gains without domain adaptation.
